content.text: Uniform circular motion requires a net force of constant magnitude directed at the centre of the circle - the centripetal force.
The velocity in uniform circular motion is always tangential to the circle, and it is perpendicular to the radius (and therefore to the centripetal force) at the point where the body is.
Check each diagram against both requirements: $F$ must point to the centre of the orbit and $v$ must be tangent to the orbit at the marked point, so the two arrows must be at right angles.
A

The only force acting on the satellite is its gravitational attraction to Earth, so the net force $F$ is directed towards the centre of Earth. This is exactly the centripetal force needed to keep the satellite in its circular orbit.
The satellite's velocity $v$ is tangential to the orbit, and a body whose velocity direction is changing must have a net force perpendicular to its velocity, so $F$ and $v$ must be at right angles.

Only the first diagram shows $F$ directed towards Earth with $v$ tangent to the orbit; the others place $F$ pointing away from Earth or along the same line as $v$, which could not produce circular motion.

content.text: An astronaut set out in a spaceship from Earth orbit to travel to a distant star in our galaxy. The spaceship travelled at a speed of $0.8c$. When the spaceship reached the star the on-board clock showed the astronaut that the journey took 10 years. An identical clock remained on Earth. What time in years had elapsed on this clock when seen from the astronaut's spaceship?
The two clocks agree at departure, so the ship's reading of 10 years is the *proper* time on the clock that every other frame sees moving.

A moving clock always runs slow, so the moving clock's elapsed time is the shorter of the two. Work out which of the two clocks is the moving one in the frame of the observer named in the question, then apply $t_{\text{moving}} = t_{\text{proper}}\sqrt{1-v^{2}/c^{2}}$ and check that your value is below 10 years, not above it.
B

The question asks for the Earth clock's reading in the astronaut's (spaceship's) frame of reference. In that frame the Earth clock is the clock that is moving, and a moving clock runs slow, so the Earth clock must show less than the 10 years measured on the ship.

The trap option is 16.7 years: that is the duration of the journey measured by an observer on Earth, who sees the *ship's* clock running slow and dividing 10 years by $0.6$. It answers a different question from the one asked here.
Check the other options: 10.0 years ignores relativity altogether, and 3.6 years applies the contraction factor $0.6$ twice.

items: 1 mark: selects the value obtained by applying time dilation, $t = \frac{t_0}{\sqrt{1-v^{2}/c^{2}}}$, with $t$ as the proper time measured on the ship.

content.text: A DC generator uses a split-ring commutator, which reverses the connection to the external circuit every half revolution.
Sketch one full revolution: the trace must leave zero, rise to a maximum, return to zero, and then rise again in the same direction. It must never go to the opposite side of the time axis.
B

In a DC generator the two halves of the split-ring commutator are connected so that the connection to the external circuit reverses each time the coil passes through the vertical position. At that instant the induced emf is zero and changes sign, so the reversal keeps the output the same sign throughout.
The CRO therefore shows a train of identical positive half-sine humps, each starting and ending at zero, with no part of the trace below the time axis.

A constant non-zero level would require an emf that does not drop to zero twice per revolution; a trace that swings equally above and below the axis is the alternating output of a generator with slip rings; a square wave is not produced by a rotating coil at all.

content.text: A non-magnetic metal disk is balanced on a support as shown in the diagram below. The disk is initially stationary. A magnet is moved in a circular path just above the surface of the disk, without touching it.

content.alt_text: Diagram of a bar magnet with its N pole down, held just above a non-magnetic metal disk balanced on a support, with a dashed circular path showing the magnet's path around the disk.

content.text: As a result of this movement the disk begins to rotate in the same direction as the magnet. The observed effect demonstrates the principle most applicable to the operation of the
DC motor.
galvanometer.
generator.
induction motor.
The disk is not magnetic, so the only currents it can carry are eddy currents induced in it by the changing magnetic flux from the moving magnet.

Lenz's law says the induced currents oppose the change in flux that produced them, so the force on the disk acts along the magnet's motion. Now match that to the device whose torque comes from currents induced in a rotor by a rotating field.
D

As the magnet is moved around above the disk the magnetic flux through the disk changes, inducing eddy currents in the conducting disk. By Lenz's law the magnetic field produced by these currents opposes the change in flux, so the force on the disk is in the direction of the magnet's motion and the disk is dragged round with the magnet.

This is the operating principle of an induction (AC) motor: a rotating magnetic field induces currents in a rotor, and the interaction produces a torque that turns the rotor in the same direction as the field.
A DC motor, a generator and a galvanometer all require a current supplied through a coil, brushes and a commutator, so none of them is driven by induced currents alone.

items: 1 mark: selects the device whose operation depends on the relative motion between a magnetic field and a conductor producing induced (eddy) currents that oppose the change in flux (Lenz's law).

content.text: When the switch is closed, a current $I$ flows around the loop. Which of the following diagrams most closely represents the final shape of the loop after the switch is closed?

content.text: The two straight leads to the fixed terminals cannot change shape, so ask which sections of the loop are free to move and which forces act on them.

For a current-carrying loop, consider the forces on pairs of opposite, parallel sections. They act in equal and opposite pairs, so the net force on the loop is zero only for the shape that keeps this symmetry. Choose that option.
A

When the switch is closed a current flows around the loop and every section of it experiences a magnetic force. In a symmetric shape each section has an opposite, parallel counterpart carrying current in the opposite sense, so the mutual forces are equal and opposite and the resultant on the loop is zero.
A circle has that symmetry for every pair of elements, so the loop experiences no net force and keeps its original shape.

In the cross, four-lobed and tall-rectangle shapes the parallel sections are not paired symmetrically, so the forces do not cancel. Each of those shapes would have to move to a different shape before forces balanced, so none is the final shape.

content.text: Which of the following did the Braggs investigate using X-ray diffraction?
Cathode rays
Crystal structure
Photoelectric effect
Superconductivity
X-rays have wavelengths comparable to the spacing of atoms in a crystal, so they are diffracted by the regularly spaced planes of atoms.

The angles at which the diffracted beams appear give the distances between those planes, which is a measurement of the internal arrangement of a solid rather than of charge, emission of electrons or resistance.
B

Bragg's law, $n\lambda = 2d\sin\theta$, relates the angle at which X-rays are diffracted by the parallel planes of atoms in a crystal to the plane spacing $d$. Measuring those angles for many sets of planes gives the crystal structure, which is what the Braggs investigated.

Cathode rays are streams of electrons accelerated from a cathode, the photoelectric effect is the emission of electrons from a metal by incident light, and superconductivity is the drop to zero electrical resistance. None of these was studied with X-ray diffraction.

items: 1 mark: selects crystal structure, since Bragg diffraction of X-rays by crystal planes was used to determine atomic spacings and crystal geometry.

Cathode rays pass through metals.
Cathode rays are charged particles.
Cathode rays travel in straight lines.
Look closely at the edges of the shadow: are they sharp or blurred? A sharp shadow means the beam did not spread as it travelled across the tube.
A statement about what cathode rays can pass *through* is not what a shadow experiment can test. Choose the statement that describes the shape of the beam itself.

The Maltese cross casts a sharp, well-defined shadow with clear edges. The only way a solid obstacle produces such a clean shadow is if the cathode rays travel in straight lines from the cathode to the fluorescent screen, so any obstruction in their path blocks them cleanly.

The experiment does not test whether the rays can pass through glass or metals, because the tube walls and the cross itself both block them. It also gives no information about charge, which requires deflection by electric and magnetic fields.

content.text: An n-type semiconductor is produced when silicon crystal is doped with small quantities of phosphorus. How will this doping change the crystal's electrical conductivity?
The conductivity will decrease because there are fewer holes in the valence band.
The conductivity will increase because there are more holes in the valence band.
The conductivity will decrease because there are fewer electrons in the conduction band.
The conductivity will increase because there are more electrons in the conduction band.
Silicon has four valence electrons while phosphorus has five. Ask what happens to the extra electron: can it stay bound in the outer shell, or does it become free to move through the crystal?

A free electron in the conduction band is a charge carrier, and more carriers means lower resistance. Decide which band the donated electrons occupy and in which direction the conductivity therefore changes.
D
Each phosphorus atom has a fifth valence electron that is only weakly bound to the silicon lattice. It is promoted to the conduction band, where it moves freely through the crystal.

These free electrons are the majority charge carriers, so their concentration increases and the conductivity increases. Doping with an element having fewer valence electrons would instead create holes in the valence band, so both options referring to holes are wrong, as is the option claiming a decrease.

items: 1 mark: selects the option stating that conductivity increases because extra electrons are promoted into the conduction band, where many more charge carriers are available.

content.text: A glass sheet was placed between the transmitter and receiver. Which of the following observations is consistent with the photoelectric effect that Hertz produced?
Radio waves were blocked when the glass sheet was in place.
Ultraviolet waves were blocked when the glass sheet was in place.
The maximum spark length was longer when the glass sheet was in place.
The maximum spark length was shorter when the glass sheet was in place.
Ordinary glass transmits visible light and radio waves but absorbs ultraviolet. The receiver in Hertz's set-up works by photoelectric emission of electrons from the spark gap.
Ask how the size of the spark depends on whether electrons are being ejected from the receiver electrodes, and then which way that size changes when the ultraviolet is removed.
D

Glass transmits radio waves, so the radiation still reaches the receiver, but it absorbs the ultraviolet component. The ultraviolet is what ejects electrons from the receiver's electrodes by the photoelectric effect, and those electrons are what allow the gap to discharge and produce a spark.
With the ultraviolet removed no photoelectrons are released, the gap conducts less easily and the maximum spark length is shorter.
Blocking the radio waves would require a conductor rather than glass, and the spark length increasing with the glass in place contradicts the removal of the photoelectrons.

items: 1 mark: selects the observation that the maximum spark length is shorter with the glass in place, since glass absorbs ultraviolet radiation and prevents it ejecting electrons from the receiver electrodes.

content.text: The electric field between the plates has a magnitude of $200\,\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$. The magnetic field is adjusted so that the ion passes through undeflected. What is the magnitude of the adjusted magnetic field, and the polarity of the M terminal relative to the N terminal?
Polarity of M relative to N: positive; magnitude of magnetic field: $0.8\,\mathrm{T}$
Polarity of M relative to N: negative; magnitude of magnetic field: $0.8\,\mathrm{T}$
Polarity of M relative to N: positive; magnitude of magnetic field: $1.25\,\mathrm{T}$
Polarity of M relative to N: negative; magnitude of magnetic field: $1.25\,\mathrm{T}$
For the ion to pass through undeflected the magnetic force $qvB$ and the electric force $qE$ must be equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.

Use the right-hand rule for a positive charge moving to the right with the field into the page to find which way the magnetic force acts. The electric force must oppose it, and remember an electric field points from the positive plate to the negative plate.
A

Direction: for a positive ion moving to the right with $\mathbf{B}$ directed into the page, $\mathbf{F} = q\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B}$ points upward. The electric force must therefore point downward, so the field points downward from M to N, which makes the upper plate M positive relative to N.

The value $1.25\,\mathrm{T}$ comes from inverting the ratio ($v/E$ instead of $E/v$), and choosing the opposite polarity would leave the two forces acting in the same direction rather than cancelling.

content.text: The experiment was repeated with the ball leaving the table at different speeds. Graph the relationship between the range and the horizontal speed at $Y$. Identify on your graph the results from the first trial.

Before drawing anything, work out how the range depends on the horizontal speed. The height of the table is the same in every trial, so the time the ball takes to reach the floor is the same in every trial, and the range is that fixed time multiplied by the horizontal speed. Ask what that implies about the shape of the graph and about where the line starts.

Plot range on the vertical axis and the horizontal speed at $Y$ on the horizontal axis, both with units, then use the first trial's data, $(1.85,\,0.60)$, to check that your line passes through the right place.
A straight line through the origin with the first-trial point $(1.85\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},\,0.60\,\mathrm{m})$ marked on it.

The shape of the graph follows from the independence of the horizontal and vertical motion. Vertically the ball leaves the table at $Y$ with zero vertical velocity and falls from the table height $h$, so $h = \frac{1}{2}gt^{2}$ and $t = \sqrt{2h/g}$. The apparatus is unchanged between trials, so $h$ is a constant and so is $t$. Horizontally the speed is constant all the way from $Y$ to the floor, so the range is the horizontal speed multiplied by that fixed time, that is, direct proportionality.

The graph is therefore a straight line through the origin, of gradient equal to the time of flight, and the first trial's point $(1.85\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},\,0.60\,\mathrm{m})$ has to sit on it. The first trial is also a consistency check on the data: $0.60/1.85 = 0.324\,\mathrm{s}$ implies a table height of $0.51\,\mathrm{m}$, which is reasonable. A graph that is straight but does not pass through the origin, or one that curves because the student has assumed the horizontal speed changes during the fall, loses the relationship mark; the commonest single loss is omitting the units from the axes.

2 marks: correctly labelled axes (including units) AND (a straight line approaching the origin OR the point $(1.85,\,0.6)$ identified).
1 mark: correctly labelled axes (units not required) OR a straight line approaching the origin OR the point $(1.85,\,0.6)$ identified.

content.text: The apparatus described in this first-hand investigation was used to carry out an identical experiment on another planet where the acceleration due to gravity is less than that on Earth. The horizontal speed of the ball as it left the table on the planet was the same as in part (a). Compare the range of the ball on the planet to that on Earth. Explain your answer.

The horizontal speed at $Y$ is the same on the planet as on Earth, so the range can only differ if the time of flight differs. From $t = \sqrt{2h/g}$ decide which way the time of flight changes when $g$ is smaller, holding the table height fixed.
Then check the direction of your answer against the graph from part (b): the gradient of range against speed is the time of flight, so a larger gradient means a larger range for the same speed.
The range on the planet is longer than on Earth because $g$ is smaller, so the time of flight is longer.

The vertical motion is unaffected by the horizontal speed, so on the planet $t = \sqrt{2h/g}$ with the same table height $h$ but a smaller $g$. A smaller $g$ gives a longer time of flight: if $g$ were half the Earth's value, $t$ would increase by $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.4$. Since $\text{range} = v_x t$ and $v_x$ is unchanged at $1.85\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, the range on the planet is larger than the $0.60\,\mathrm{m}$ measured on Earth.

In terms of the graph from part (b) the comparison is simply that the line is steeper on the planet, because its gradient is the time of flight. Two marks require the comparison and the reason; a response that says only 'the range is longer', or only 'the gravity is smaller', earns one.

content.text: Discuss the effect of Earth's rotational motion on the launch of this satellite.

The satellite is already moving before the rocket fires, because the launch site is carried round by the Earth's rotation. Which direction of launch gives the satellite the largest share of the speed it already has?
Then connect the direction to the practical consequence: what does the rocket no longer have to supply, and how does that translate into fuel?
Satellites are launched towards the east so that Earth's rotation already gives the satellite part of the speed it needs, reducing the fuel required.

Points on the Earth's surface, including points on the equator, already travel eastwards at about $460\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ because the Earth rotates once every 24 hours. A satellite launched eastwards therefore leaves the surface with that velocity already added to its own, and the rocket only has to supply the difference. The orbital speed required for this orbit is $v = \sqrt{GM_{E}/r} = 7.3\times10^{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, so an eastward launch saves some $460\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ of the change in speed needed, about 6%, and because the fuel required by a rocket is proportional to the change in speed the saving in fuel is of the same order. A satellite launched westwards must first be slowed down against the Earth's rotation before it can reach orbit, so it requires more fuel.

The single mark is earned by identifying the issue, assistance to the satellite's motion or reduced fuel usage, AND relating it to the direction of launch, as the mark scheme requires. Either half on its own is not enough, and a response that merely says the Earth rotates without the connection to the launch direction does not earn the mark.

content.text: Outline TWO features of the aether model for the transmission of light.

The question is about the model, not about the material. Two features of the *model* are required: what light was said to need in order to travel, and what the model said about the frame of reference in which light's speed has its single true value.

Avoid answering with physical properties of aether on their own. The 2003 guidelines record that candidates who listed properties such as rigidity or low density instead of features of the model did not attract the second mark.
Aether was the medium through which light propagated, and it was a rigid, incompressible frame of reference absolutely at rest relative to which all other frames moved.

Start from what the wave model of light requires. A wave needs a medium, so the first feature of the model is that light is a mechanical wave which propagates through the all-pervading aether. The second feature is the model's distinctive assumption: the aether is a single preferred frame of reference, absolutely at rest, and the speed of light is $c$ only relative to that frame. This immediately implies that an observer moving through the aether should measure a different speed of light along the direction of motion, which is exactly what part (b) sets out to test. Both features are therefore statements about the model, not about the mechanical properties of a substance.

content.text: Recount the Michelson and Morley experiment, which attempted to measure the relative velocity of Earth through the aether, and describe the results they anticipated.
Write this as a numbered sequence: what was constructed, what was observed, what was changed, and what the aether model predicted. Use the phrase 'interference pattern' for the observation.

The predicted result has to follow from the model. If the aether exists, the time taken by light to travel out and back along the arm that lies along Earth's direction of motion should differ from the time along the arm at right angles to it, and rotating the apparatus swaps which arm is which.
A neat, labelled diagram of the interferometer is worth credit in its own right, so sketch the beam splitter, the two perpendicular arms, the mirrors and the observation point.

Michelson and Morley split a single beam of light into two beams travelling along perpendicular equal-length arms of an interferometer, reflected them back to recombine and observed an interference pattern. They expected the pattern to shift when the apparatus was rotated through $90^\circ$, because Earth's motion through the aether would change the effective speed of light along and across the direction of motion.

Step 1, the apparatus: a single beam of light is split at a beam splitter into two beams, which are sent along two arms of equal length at right angles to each other, reflected by mirrors at the far ends and recombined at the beam splitter. Step 2, the observation: where the returning beams overlap they interfere, and a pattern of light and dark fringes is seen. Step 3, the procedure: the apparatus is rotated through $90^{\circ}$ about its vertical axis, so the two arms exchange their positions relative to the direction of Earth's motion through the aether, and the pattern is examined again. Step 4, the anticipated result: the two patterns should differ. The reasoning is that, in the aether frame, the light travelling along the direction of Earth's motion has an effective forward speed of $c + v$ and a return speed of $c - v$, while the light travelling across that direction has an effective speed of $c$, so the two paths no longer take the same time and the optical path difference changes. Rotating the apparatus changes which arm has which of these effective speeds, so the fringes must shift. (The null result that Michelson and Morley actually obtained is the point of the question but is not what part (b) asks for.)

content.text: A current of $2$ amperes flows from the battery. Calculate the magnitude and direction of the initial force on each wire.
The field that one wire experiences is produced by the other wire, so $B = \dfrac{\mu_{0}I}{2\pi r}$ with $r$ set by the separation of the wires and $I$ the current in the other wire.

The force on the straight section of the wire follows from $F = BIl$ since the wire is perpendicular to the field ($\sin 90^{\circ} = 1$). Convert both the $35\,\mathrm{cm}$ length and the $1.5\,\mathrm{cm}$ separation into metres before substituting.

For the direction, use the right-hand grip rule twice: once for the field produced by each wire at the position of the other, and once for the force on each wire. As a check, parallel currents in the same direction attract.
$F \approx 1.9\times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{N}$ on each wire, directed away from the other wire (repulsive).

Trace the circuit first. A single cell bridges the two wires at the top (see the figure), so the current leaves one terminal, runs down one wire, crosses the conducting salt solution at the bottom of the beaker and returns up the other wire. The two straight vertical sections therefore carry equal currents of $2.0\,\mathrm{A}$ in OPPOSITE directions. The stipulation that the wire ends do not touch the bottom of the beaker is what guarantees the circuit closes through the solution alone.

with $r = 0.015\,\mathrm{m}$ the separation of the wires and $l = 0.35\,\mathrm{m}$ the straight length of each wire above the solution. Antiparallel currents repel, so each wire is pushed away from the other and the two wires move apart; the old stored answer's 'attractive' was the result of applying the parallel-currents-attract rule without checking the current directions.

content.text: Explain the effect of the motion of the magnet on the solenoid in the two investigations.
Both investigations involve the same changing flux through the coil, so start by asking, in each case, whether an induced current is actually able to flow.
An emf is induced whenever the flux changes, but a current only flows if the circuit is complete. No current means no induced magnetic field, and therefore no force and no motion of the solenoid.

In the second investigation the induced current must oppose the change that produced it (Lenz's law). Decide which end of the solenoid becomes a north pole, then use the right-hand grip rule to fix the direction the solenoid moves.

Investigation 1: an EMF is induced in the solenoid but no current flows (open circuit), so there is no induced magnetic field and the solenoid does not move. Investigation 2: the closed copper wire allows an induced current to flow; by Lenz's law the induced field opposes the increasing flux from the approaching magnet, so the solenoid is repelled and moves to the LEFT.

Investigation 1: since the solenoid is not in a closed circuit, no current can be induced by the changing magnetic field. No current means no induced magnetic field and therefore no force and no motion. Investigation 2: the circuit is closed, so the magnet induces a current in the solenoid. Lenz's law states that the induced current produces a magnetic field opposing the changing field that induced it, so the solenoid's field opposes the magnet's field. content.text: Explain the relationship between the current in the primary coil and the current in the secondary coil of an ideal step-down transformer in relation to the conservation of energy.
For an ideal transformer nothing is lost, so the power into the primary must equal the power out of the secondary: $V_pI_p = V_sI_s$.
Then bring in the turns relation $V_p/V_s = N_p/N_s$. Decide which voltage is the larger for a step-down transformer, and let conservation of energy fix which current is the larger.
Conservation of energy requires $V_p I_p = V_s I_s$, so $I_s > I_p$: the current in the secondary coil is greater than that in the primary coil, and the ratio follows the inverse of the turns ratio.

Write conservation of energy for the transformer as a power balance. The power delivered to the primary coil is $V_pI_p$ and, in the ideal case, all of it is delivered by the secondary coil, so $V_pI_p = V_sI_s$. A step-down transformer has $N_p > N_s$, and because the voltage ratio equals the turns ratio, $V_p > V_s$. Substituting, $I_s = I_p\,V_p/V_s$, and since $V_p/V_s > 1$ it follows that $I_s > I_p$. content.text: Explain why a transformer will work in an AC circuit but not in a DC circuit.
Begin from $|\varepsilon| = N|\Delta\Phi/\Delta t|$. A secondary emf needs a changing flux, so ask separately what an AC primary current does to the core flux and what a DC primary current does.
Adding the switching case shows the difference cleanly: a DC supply produces a brief pulse of induced emf only at the instant it is switched on or off, and nothing at all once it is steady.

A transformer requires a changing magnetic flux through its coils to induce an emf. An AC primary current produces a changing flux, but a steady DC primary current produces constant flux, so no secondary emf and no secondary current are produced.

The law of electromagnetic induction, $|\varepsilon| = N|\Delta\Phi/\Delta t|$, says that the emf induced in the secondary coil is proportional to the rate of change of flux linking it, so a secondary voltage and current exist only while the flux through the secondary is changing. In the primary, an alternating current produces an alternating magnetomotive force, the flux in the core alternates with it, and $\Delta\Phi/\Delta t$ is continuously non-zero, so a secondary emf is induced and a secondary current flows. With direct current the primary magnetomotive force is constant; after the short transient at switch-on the core flux is constant, $\Delta\Phi/\Delta t = 0$, so no emf is induced and no secondary current flows. The corollary is that a DC supply gives a single induced pulse when it is connected and another when it is disconnected, and nothing in between.

On the sketch label the coil, the magnet, the north and south poles, the measuring device and the connecting leads. Varying the magnetic field strength. content.text: The key is the superconducting state: zero resistance and expulsion of magnetic flux (the Meissner effect), which is produced by persistent screening currents in the surface of the disk.

Use the direction rule for induced currents to fix the sense of those screening currents, and hence the direction of the force on the magnet. Then say explicitly that the magnet is stationary, so the upward magnetic force must equal the weight.

Below the critical temperature the superconductor excludes magnetic flux (Meissner effect), so the approaching magnet induces screening currents in the superconductor which produce a magnetic field opposing the magnet's field. The resulting upward repulsive force balances the magnet's weight force, so the magnet hovers.

Below the critical temperature the disk is superconducting: its electrical resistance is zero and it expels magnetic flux from its interior, the Meissner effect. The flux exclusion is produced by persistent screening currents induced in the surface layers of the disk, and by the direction rule their field opposes the magnet's field where the disk sits. The force the magnet experiences is therefore repulsive and directed away from the disk, that is vertically upwards. Because the magnet hovers it is in equilibrium, so the upward magnetic force on it is exactly equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the gravitational force, $F_{\text{mag}} = F_g$. The 2003 guidelines award full marks for stating both that the superconductor's field interacts with and opposes the magnet's field (and that a current in the superconducting state produces that field) and that the magnetic force balances gravity in the opposite direction.

content.text: Compare the model for the conduction of electricity in metals at room temperature with the model for conduction of electricity in superconductors below the critical temperature.
Set the two models out in the same order before comparing them: what carries the charge, what happens to those charge carriers in the lattice, and what happens to the energy that is supplied.
Three marks come from one similarity plus two differences, or from three clean differences. Write each point as an explicit comparison, for example 'in a metal ... whereas in a superconductor ...'.

Similarity: in both cases the current is carried by mobile electrons. Difference 1: in a room-temperature metal electrons are scattered by lattice vibrations and impurities, giving resistance and Joule heating, whereas in a superconductor below the critical temperature electrons form pairs that are not scattered. Difference 2: a metal has a small but non-zero resistance and dissipates energy, while a superconductor has zero resistance and carries current without dissipation.

Similarity: the charge carrier is the same in both cases, mobile conduction electrons, and in both the electrons drift in response to an applied electric field. First difference, resistance and dissipation: in a metal at room temperature the conduction electrons are continuously scattered by the thermal vibrations of the lattice ions and by impurity atoms, the energy lost in those collisions is dissipated as Joule heat, and this gives a small but non-zero resistance; in a superconductor below the critical temperature the electrons are not scattered in this way, so the resistance is zero and a current flows with no energy loss. Second difference, temperature dependence: a metal's resistance rises as its temperature rises, so it conducts less well when hot, whereas a superconductor conducts only below its critical temperature and reverts to normal resistive behaviour when heated above it. The 2003 guidelines award the full three marks for one similarity and two differences stated as explicit comparisons, or for three differences, or for three similarities.

content.text: Outline Thomson's experiment to measure the charge/mass ratio of an electron.

Build the experiment in two stages. First, adjust the crossed electric and magnetic fields until the electron beam passes through undeflected, which fixes the speed of the electrons; then remove the electric field and let the magnetic field alone curve the beam, measuring the radius of the path.

The undeflected condition $qE = qvB$ gives $v$, and the curved path gives a centripetal force $qvB$ on an electron of mass $m$ moving at radius $r$. It is the combination of the two stages that yields $q/m$, so make the link between them explicit rather than leaving the two results side by side.

Electrons were accelerated from a cathode through a potential difference $V$ to give them speed $v$, and passed undeflected through a crossed electric field $E$ and magnetic field $B$ ($E = vB$). With the fields switched off, the electron beam traced a circular arc of radius $r$ in the magnetic field alone, giving $r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$. Since $v$ is known from $qV = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}$, the ratio $\dfrac{q}{m} = \dfrac{2V}{rB^{2}}$ follows.

content.text: When the laser light was shone onto a photo-cell, no current was detected. The student increased the intensity of the light but still detected no current. Explain this observation.

Emission of a photoelectron requires a minimum energy in a single photon, because the electron has to escape the metal's surface. Compare the energy of one photon from this laser, from part (a), with that threshold.

Then separate the two quantities that can be adjusted: the number of photons arriving each second, and the energy carried by each photon. Only one of them decides whether electrons are emitted at all, and the other only decides how many.

The energy of each infrared photon ($1.28\times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$) is below the work function of the photo-cell, so no photoelectrons are emitted. Increasing the intensity increases the number of photons per second but not the energy of each photon, so no current is detected.

The photoelectric effect has a threshold: an electron is only released if a single photon delivers at least the work function $\phi$ of the metal, $hf \geq \phi$. Part (a) gives the energy of one infrared photon from this laser as $1.28\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$, which is below the work function of the photo-cathode, so the threshold frequency is higher than the frequency of this laser. No electrons are emitted, so no photocurrent is detected. The student's second attempt changes only the intensity. Since the total energy delivered per second is $Nhf$, raising the intensity increases the number of photons $N$ striking the surface each second but leaves the energy of each photon, $hf$, unchanged. The per-photon threshold is therefore still not met and no current flows. The observation is exactly what the quantum model of light predicts: the photocurrent depends on frequency, not on intensity, and increasing the brightness of a beam below threshold produces no current at all.

content.text: Describe Einstein's contributions to Special Relativity and to Quantum Theory and how these contributions changed the direction of scientific thinking in the Twentieth Century.

The question has two halves and a linking clause. For each of special relativity and quantum theory, name the specific contribution, then state which classical assumption it replaced — that second step is what earns the marks for changing the direction of scientific thinking.

For the relativity half, the shift is from absolute space and time to a frame-dependent space-time. For the quantum half, the shift is from light as a continuous wave to light as discrete quanta, and look for the practical technology that followed directly from the quantum contribution.

Special Relativity: Einstein proposed in 1905 that the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames and that the speed of light is invariant, from which he derived time dilation, length contraction and $E = mc^{2}$; this replaced absolute space and time with a relativistic space-time and ultimately led to nuclear energy. Quantum Theory: he explained the photoelectric effect (1905) by proposing that light consists of photons of energy $E = hf$, and in 1917 proposed that atoms absorb and emit light only in quanta, with spontaneous and stimulated emission; this replaced the classical wave picture of light with a quantum one and led to lasers and quantum theory. Together these changes moved physics from absolute classical frameworks to relativistic and quantised descriptions of space, time and matter.

Special relativity (1905). Einstein proposed that the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames of reference and that the speed of light in vacuum has the same value for all inertial observers, independent of the motion of the source. From these postulates he derived time dilation, length contraction and the relation $E = mc^{2}$.

How this changed thinking. It replaced the Newtonian framework of absolute space and absolute time, in which space and time are the same for everyone, with a single relativistic space-time in which both depend on the motion of the observer. It also made mass and energy equivalent, so that $E = mc^{2}$ became the basis of nuclear physics and the explanation of the energy source of stars and of nuclear reactions, and it showed that the speed of light sets an absolute speed limit for any massive object.

Quantum theory. In 1905 Einstein explained the photoelectric effect by proposing that light consists of photons with energy $E = hf$, and in 1917 he proposed that atoms absorb and emit light in discrete quanta, distinguishing spontaneous emission from stimulated emission.

How this changed thinking. It replaced the classical wave picture of light with a quantum one in which light behaves as particles, and it established that atoms interact with radiation in discrete amounts. The idea of stimulated emission led directly to masers and lasers, and the quantised energy levels of the atom became the foundation of the quantum description of matter. Together the two contributions moved physics from absolute classical frameworks to relativistic and quantised descriptions of space, time and matter, and both were experimental ideas that redirected twentieth-century physics.

content.text: In a particle accelerator called a synchrotron, magnetic fields are used to control the motion of an electron so that it follows a circular path of fixed radius. Describe the changes required in the magnetic field to accelerate an electron to near the speed of light. Support your answer with appropriate mathematical relationships.

The radius of the path is fixed by the design of the machine, so ask how the magnetic force $F = qvB$ must change to keep supplying the increasing centripetal force $\dfrac{mv^{2}}{r}$ as the speed grows.
Eliminate $F$ between $qvB = \dfrac{mv^{2}}{r}$ and write $B$ explicitly in terms of $v$, $q$, $r$ and $m$. That expression alone tells you the trend.
Then consider what happens to $m$ as $v$ approaches $c$, using $m = \dfrac{m_{0}}{\sqrt{1 - v^{2}/c^{2}}}$, and how much faster than linearly the field would then have to grow.

The magnetic field must be increased continuously, in step with the electron's speed. Since $F = qvB$ and $F = \dfrac{mv^{2}}{r}$, with $r$ fixed, $B = \dfrac{mv}{qr}$: even without relativistic effects $B$ rises linearly with $v$, and as $v \to c$ the relativistic mass $m = \dfrac{m_0}{\sqrt{1-v^{2}/c^{2}}}$ grows without bound, so $B$ must grow very rapidly.

content.text: Summarise the geophysical evidence that supports the theory of plate tectonics.
Give each item as an observation plus the plate-tectonic process it supports, rather than as a bare fact.
The magnetic stripes in the ocean floor and the distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes are the two that are unambiguously geophysical - use those first if you are short of time.
Three distinct pieces of evidence reach the top band; two discussed in depth also reach it.

Palaeomagnetism: matching patterns of magnetic stripes in matching rock formations on either side of ocean ridges, with ages increasing away from the ridge. Seafloor spreading: new ocean crust is created at mid-ocean ridges and moves away from them. Fit of continents: continental shelves and matching rock sequences line up across ocean basins. Earthquake and volcano distribution: these are concentrated along plate boundaries rather than randomly. Fossil and climate evidence: identical fossil and glacial deposits occur in matching rocks on now widely separated continents.

items: Palaeomagnetism: reversals of the Earth's magnetic field are recorded in cooled rock as alternating stripes of magnetised basalt, and matching stripes of the same age occur on opposite sides of a ridge - so new ocean crust must be created at the ridge and carried outwards.

Seafloor spreading: the age of ocean crust increases with distance from a mid-ocean ridge and the youngest crust is always at the ridge axis, which is only consistent with creation at the ridge and outward migration.
Fit of continents and matching rock sequences: continental shelves, mountain belts and rock strata line up across ocean basins, so the continents were once joined.

Earthquake and volcano distribution: shallow-focus earthquakes, deep ocean trenches and active volcanoes trace narrow belts that follow the edges of the plates rather than being scattered randomly, so the plates have rigid interiors bounded by mobile edges.
Fossil and climate evidence: identical fossils and glacial deposits occur in matching rock sequences on now widely separated continents, so the land masses were joined when those organisms lived.

content.text: Outline the structure and function of a geophone. (2 marks)
For the geophone, identify what is stationary and what moves relative to it, and what electrical quantity that relative motion produces.
On the travel-time graph the two lines cross because one wave has the faster speed but the greater initial delay - ask which of them has further to travel at short distances.
For the speed, remember the graph plots time against distance, so the gradient is the reciprocal of the speed and has to be inverted.

A geophone contains a magnet suspended by a spring inside a coil. When a seismic wave passes, the case moves relative to the magnet and coil, so the relative motion changes the magnetic flux through the coil and induces a small emf, and hence a current, which the seismograph records. (d)

The essential physics is relative motion between a conductor and a magnetic field. A spring holds the magnet (or the coil) so that its inertia prevents it following the ground; electromagnetic induction then converts that relative motion into a measurable current.

content.text: Outline the application of Newton's theory of universal gravitation to the field of geophysics, and discuss how information obtained from gravity surveys has led to a greater understanding of the structure of Earth.
This part has two halves joined by one link: state Newton's law, say how $g$ is measured locally, and then say what that measurement reveals.
The link is density: because $g$ depends on the mass and therefore the density of the material beneath a point, a departure from the expected value means the structure is not what was assumed.
For the top band, name the concrete things gravity surveys have mapped - not just 'hidden structure'.

Newton's law of universal gravitation, $F = \dfrac{GMm}{r^{2}}$, gives the gravitational force between masses, so geophysicists can predict the gravitational field produced by known rock types. In practice gravimeters (and satellite tracking) are used to measure the local gravitational field very precisely. Because $g$ depends on the mass, and therefore the density, of the material beneath a point, differences between the measured value and the value expected for a uniform Earth (gravity anomalies) reveal variations in density and hence in structure. Mapping these anomalies has shown the shape of the crust, the thickness and location of sedimentary basins, the extent of concealed faults and ore bodies, and the thickness of the oceanic crust - features that could not be observed directly, so gravity surveying has become one of the main tools for mapping hidden structure of Earth.

Both halves must be present. The application half: state $F = \dfrac{GMm}{r^{2}}$, or equivalently $g = \dfrac{GM}{r^{2}}$, and that geophysicists measure the local gravitational field very precisely with gravimeters, or infer it from satellite motion.

The understanding half: because $g$ depends on the density of the material below a point, differences between the measured value and that expected for a uniform Earth are gravity anomalies, and mapping them reveals the shape of the crust, the thickness and location of sedimentary basins, the extent of concealed faults and ore bodies, and the thickness of oceanic crust - none of which can be observed directly.

The 7-8 mark band requires all of: the statement of the law, the measurement of the local field, the connection to density and structure, and the point that the information concerns structure that other methods cannot easily reach.

content.text: Identify the property of the hydrogen nucleus that makes it useful in magnetic resonance imaging.
For MRI, ask what the hydrogen nucleus must be able to do in a strong external field for the technique to work at all.
For the X-ray tube, account for the energy: an electron is given kinetic energy by the accelerating voltage, so where does that energy go when the electron reaches the anode?
There are two contributions to the X-ray beam. One produces a continuous range of photon energies and the other produces only a few discrete lines.
The hydrogen nucleus (a single proton) behaves like a small magnet because it has a nuclear spin and hence a magnetic moment. (a)

The requirement is that the nucleus respond to an applied field. The proton has a magnetic moment associated with its spin, so in a strong field it aligns parallel or antiparallel, with slightly more nuclei parallel, and a net magnetisation is produced. That is the property MRI uses.

content.text: Describe how X-rays are produced when electrons strike the anode in an X-ray tube.

Electrons are accelerated through a high potential difference and their kinetic energy is converted into X-ray photons when they strike the anode, by two processes: bremsstrahlung, in which an electron is decelerated and emits a continuous spectrum of X-rays, and excitation of inner-shell atoms of the anode, which then emit characteristic X-rays as the electrons fall back to lower energy levels.

Both required points are the conversion of the electrons' kinetic energy into X-rays, and the excitation of inner-shell anode atoms followed by emission as those electrons fall back to lower levels. The characteristic line X-rays come from the second process and the continuous bremsstrahlung radiation from the first; naming only one of the two earns 1 mark.

content.text: Outline the production of gamma rays and their use in the diagnostic procedure of positron emission tomography (PET).
Track the sequence: what the radiopharmaceutical emits, what that particle then does in the tissue, and what the detectors register as a result.
The arrangement of the detectors is the clue - why must two detectors on opposite sides of the body fire at the same time?
Think about how much of the radiation reaches a detector depending on how much tissue lies in its path.

A radiopharmaceutical administered to the patient emits positrons. Each positron annihilates with an electron in the tissue to produce two gamma rays travelling in opposite directions. Ring detectors placed on opposite sides of the body detect these gamma rays in coincidence; because the gamma rays are attenuated by different amounts depending on the depth of tissue they must traverse, the coincidence data locate the concentration of the radiopharmaceutical and build up a PET image.

Method: work outwards from the event to the image. Identify the emitted particle, then what happens to it in the tissue, then what the detector registers, then how position information is recovered. Do not skip the annihilation step - without it there is no explanation of why gamma rays appear at all.

Why the two gamma rays travel in opposite directions: the electron and positron annihilate essentially at rest in the tissue, so momentum conservation requires the two photons to be emitted back to back, each with an energy of $0.511\,\mathrm{MeV}$.

Why the detectors are paired: a coincidence requirement rejects the large number of unrelated single detections, so a recorded pair fixes the line of response along which the annihilation occurred. Several such lines from many events are back-projected by a computer to build up the distribution of the radiopharmaceutical.

Why the image can have depth information at all: gamma rays are attenuated by the tissue they traverse, so a detector pair on opposite sides of the body registers less radiation the more material the photons have passed through, and the amount of intervening tissue becomes a measure of how deep the source lies.

Marking: annihilation plus paired opposite detectors earns 2 marks; either on its own earns 1 mark; the 3-mark band additionally needs the radiopharmaceutical producing positrons and the attenuation-depth point.

2 marks: gamma rays are produced by electron/positron annihilation AND pairs of gamma rays are detected on opposite sides of the body.
1 mark: gamma rays are produced by electron/positron annihilation OR pairs of gamma rays are detected on opposite sides of the body.

Describe how a bone scan is able to provide information that an X-ray cannot provide.

The radiopharmaceutical is tagged with an isotope that is selectively taken up by bone and by areas of changed bone metabolism, so the scan shows the function (physiology) of the bone, revealing early or diffuse changes such as metastases. An X-ray shows only the anatomy, so it may show no abnormality at all.

content.text: Ultrasound travelling through kidney tissue in the body encounters a different type of tissue. Identify the type of tissue that will result in the greatest proportion of the incident pulse being reflected at the boundary between the kidney and the other tissue. Justify your choice.
Fat, because it has the greatest difference in acoustic impedance compared with kidney, so the greatest proportion of the incident pulse is reflected at the kidney/fat boundary. (d)

The proportion of an incident pulse reflected at a boundary depends on the mismatch in impedance there, not on the absolute values. The impedances are fat $1.38\times10^{6}$, blood $1.61\times10^{6}$, kidney $1.62\times10^{6}$, liver $1.65\times10^{6}$ and muscle $1.70\times10^{6}\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$, so fat, which is $0.24\times10^{6}$ away from kidney, is by far the greatest mismatch and the greatest proportion of the pulse is reflected.

content.text: Describe the properties of ultrasound that led to its use in the measurement of bone density.

Ultrasound can be passed right through the bone from an emitter on one side to a detector on the other. Variations in bone density give the bone a different acoustic impedance, so reflection from a healthy bone/flesh boundary differs from reflection from an abnormal one and the transmitted intensity differs. The speed of ultrasound also differs in bones of different density, so both timing and intensity measurements give the bone density.

Three points earn 3 marks: ultrasound passes through the bone from one side to the other, with emitter and detector on opposite sides; variations in bone density give the bone a different acoustic impedance; reflection from a healthy bone/flesh boundary differs from reflection from an abnormal bone/flesh boundary so the transmitted intensity is different; and the speed of ultrasound is different in bones of different density.

content.text: An understanding of the properties of electrons, and our ability to control their behaviour, have played key roles in the development of CAT scans and positron emission tomography imaging technologies. Justify this statement with reference to the production and display of images used for medical diagnosis.
This is a justification, not a description: every claim must be attached to a specific property of the electron and to a specific stage of the imaging process.
Cover the whole chain - production, control of the beam, detection and display - rather than concentrating on the source alone.
The display device matters as much as the beam, so do not leave it out.

The electron carries a negative charge, so it can be accelerated, deflected and focused by electric and magnetic fields, and its beam can therefore be steered to where it is needed. In CAT scanning, electrons are accelerated in an X-ray tube and controlled by electric and magnetic fields to produce a narrow X-ray beam that is rotated about the patient and detected to build a cross-sectional image. In PET, the positrons emitted by the radiopharmaceutical annihilate with electrons, and the resulting gamma rays are detected electronically. In both techniques the detection and display of the images uses electronic circuits and cathode ray tubes in which the beam of electrons is controlled by electric and magnetic fields, so the whole imaging chain depends on the properties of electrons and our ability to control them.

Method: this is a justification question, so every sentence should be of the form 'because electrons have property X, stage Y of the imaging chain works in the way it does'. Identify the stages first - production, transport and focusing, detection, processing, display - and make sure all of them are covered, because the display stage is where candidates most often run out.

The property to invoke is the negative charge. It is the reason fields can accelerate a beam, change its direction and focus it, and the reason a beam can be steered onto a chosen target rather than simply spreading out.

Testing your own answer: for each imaging chain you describe, ask whether you have named the electron property, the component that exploits it, and the stage of the chain it belongs to. A claim that cannot survive all three of those questions is not yet a justification.

Watch the sign of the claim as well. The question does not ask whether electrons are useful in these techniques - it asserts that they are, and asks for the argument. Resist describing the hardware; every point must come back to a property of the electron and to our ability to impose a field on it.

Marking: the 7-8 band needs PET and CAT both covered with the charge of the electron explicitly linked to control, and recognition of the display stage; 5-6 needs substantial knowledge applied to both; 2-4 needs at least one property or control method tied to one of the two techniques.

content.text: Define the term resolution of a telescope.
For the definition, say what the instrument must be able to do to two objects, and express that as a minimum angular separation.
For the method, the limit on a ground-based telescope comes from the atmosphere rather than from the mirror, so the correction has to act on the incoming light.
Your description should mention what is measured and what is then adjusted.

Resolution is the ability of a telescope to distinguish between two close objects or to resolve fine detail, expressed as the minimum angular separation of two objects that can just be distinguished. (a)

Resolution is a measure of how finely detail can be separated, so it is quoted as the smallest angle $\theta_{min}$ subtended by two points that can still be seen as two separate images rather than one. For a circular aperture the Rayleigh criterion gives $\theta_{min} = 1.22\lambda/D$, so for a fixed observing wavelength the resolution of a telescope improves only by increasing the diameter $D$ of its aperture.

content.text: Describe ONE method by which the resolution of a ground-based system can be improved.

Adaptive optics: measure and correct the distortions of the incoming light caused by the Earth's atmosphere, using a fast-moving mirror, so that the light reaching the telescope behaves as if the atmosphere were absent and the diffraction-limited resolution is recovered.

The limit on a ground-based telescope is set by the atmosphere rather than by the mirror: turbulence in the air distorts the wavefront arriving from a point source and spreads its image into a blur whose size is set by the seeing rather than by the diffraction limit of the aperture. Adaptive optics removes that distortion. A wavefront sensor measures the tilt and aberrations of the incoming light, usually from a laser guide star, and a deformable mirror, whose profile can be changed, is driven to flatten the wavefront again. The mirror has to be corrected fast enough to follow the changing turbulence, several hundred times per second, and the image then approaches the diffraction-limited resolution set by the aperture.

Either of two other routes would earn the 2 marks: put the telescope above most of the atmosphere, in space or on a high mountain, so the light crosses little or no air; or combine the light from widely separated apertures by interferometry, so the effective aperture is the baseline between them and $\theta_{min}$ is smaller by the same factor.

content.text: Evaluate the impact of studying the visible spectrum of light on our understanding of celestial objects.
Organise the answer around the distinct kinds of information a spectrum gives, not around the history of astronomy.
At least three ideas are needed: chemical composition, surface temperature, and either motion or distance.
For the top band, say what the information changed - how the stars went from being points of light to being measurable objects.

The visible spectrum of astronomical objects, and in particular the absorption lines in it, has had a major impact on our understanding of celestial objects. It allows the chemical composition of stars, nebulae and galaxies to be determined, since each element produces its own unique line pattern. It allows surface temperatures to be deduced from which species are ionised, and distances to be found by comparing apparent and absolute magnitudes. Finally, the red-shift of spectral lines gives the recession velocities of galaxies and quasars, which is the principal evidence that the universe is expanding. The significance of this work is that it turned the stars from uncharacterised points of light into objects whose composition, temperature, motion and distance could all be measured, laying the foundations of modern astrophysics and of the Big Bang model of the universe.

Method: since this is an evaluate question, organise the body around distinct pieces of information rather than around objects or around the history of astronomy. Each heading should be an information gain, followed by the conclusion it forces.

Four headings carry the marks, and they are worth separating explicitly because students routinely merge the first two: what the atoms are (composition, from the identity of the absorption lines); what state they are in (temperature, from which species are present and how strong their lines are); how they are moving (red-shift giving recession velocity, which is the evidence for an expanding universe); and where they are (distance, by comparing apparent with absolute magnitudes).

The physics that makes each heading possible is one idea applied repeatedly - every element has its own set of discrete energy levels, so it absorbs only at its own wavelengths. Composition, temperature and motion are all read off the same set of lines; only the interpretation changes.

The evaluation has to be argued, not listed. The closing move is to say what changed as a result: stars went from being uncharacterised points of light to objects whose composition, temperature, motion and distance could all be measured, which is what made modern astrophysics and the Big Bang model possible.
Marking: the 7-8 band needs at least three of the four headings plus the significance; 5-6 needs three headings; 3-4 needs two; 1-2 needs basic knowledge with at least two ideas.

Rutherford's model came from alpha-particle scattering through a thin foil, so ask what the rare large deflections and the rare pass-throughs forced him to propose.
Bohr's refinement answers a specific failure of that model: a charged particle accelerating in an orbit is supposed to radiate, which would make the electron spiral into the nucleus.

A small, dense, positively-charged nucleus at the centre, surrounded by electrons orbiting it. (a)

The mark is for identifying the electrons as orbiting a nucleus. The scattering evidence is that most alpha particles passed straight through, so the atom is mostly empty space, while a very small fraction were deflected through large angles or bounced back, so the positive charge and mass are concentrated in a tiny region.

content.text: Describe how Bohr refined Rutherford's model of the hydrogen atom.

Bohr proposed that electrons orbit the nucleus only in stable, discrete orbits at particular energy levels, and that electrons move between these levels by absorbing or emitting a definite amount of energy (a quantum), removing the continuous radiation that the Rutherford model would predict.

Both points are needed for 2 marks - electrons orbit only in stable discrete orbits or at quantised energy levels, AND electrons move between levels by absorbing or emitting energy. The physical point is that in each permitted orbit the electron does not radiate, and radiation is emitted or absorbed only in a transition, which is what produces line spectra.

content.text: The table below shows the different types of quarks and their charge. The standard model of matter says that protons and neutrons are composed of up and down quarks. There are three quarks in each particle.

Use the charge column to work backwards: three quarks must add up to the charge of the particle.
Try $uud$ and check the total, then $udd$ and check again.

A proton is composed of two up quarks and one down quark (uud), giving a charge of $\left(+\frac{2}{3} + \frac{2}{3} - \frac{1}{3}\right)e = +1e$. A neutron is composed of one up quark and two down quarks (udd), giving a charge of $\left(+\frac{2}{3} - \frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{3}\right)e = 0$. Both therefore have three quarks, but different combinations give a charged and an uncharged particle.

Both particles therefore contain three quarks, but different combinations give a charged and an uncharged particle. The three points that carry the marks are that protons have charge $+1$ while neutrons have zero charge, that the proton is $uud$, and that the neutron is $udd$.

content.text: Describe the requirements for a nuclear fission explosion, and describe how these are controlled in a nuclear reactor.
List the requirements for an uncontrolled chain reaction first, then ask what a reactor does about each of them.
The link between the two cases is neutron economy: what happens to the neutrons produced, and how many are needed to keep the reaction going?
Name the specific components that control the neutron population and the neutron energy in a reactor.

A nuclear fission explosion requires a large mass of fissile material such as uranium-235 or plutonium-239, a neutron source to initiate the chain reaction, and a geometry in which the critical mass is exceeded so that the majority of nuclei are close enough to absorb the emitted neutrons, with a supercritical assembly achieved rapidly. The same factors are involved in a reactor, but they are controlled so that each generation of fissions releases on average only one further fission: control rods of boron or cadmium absorb surplus neutrons to hold the reaction at the critical rate, and a moderator such as heavy water or graphite slows neutrons so that they are more likely to be absorbed by uranium-235 rather than escaping. Coolant removes the heat safely. Removing the control rods or adding moderator makes the reaction supercritical and uncontrolled, which is what happens in a bomb - the difference between the two cases is only how quickly neutrons are allowed to multiply and whether they are able to escape.

Method: this part has two halves that must both be present, and the top band depends on the explicit link between them. Write the uncontrolled case first as three requirements (fuel, initiation, geometry), then take those same three items in turn and say what a reactor does about each.

The unifying idea is neutron economy. Define the multiplication factor $k$ as the number of fissions caused by one fission. A bomb needs $k$ well above 1 and growing fast; a power reactor holds $k = 1$ on average, so each generation of fissions produces exactly one further fission in steady state.

Three consequences follow directly, and each is a separate mark: more fuel raises $\Sigma_f$; a larger assembly raises the probability $P_\text{esc}$ that a neutron stays long enough to be absorbed by another nucleus rather than escaping; and adding moderator raises $L_p$ by slowing neutrons so they are more likely to be absorbed by uranium-235 instead of being scattered out.

The controls then follow from that same equation: cadmium or boron control rods absorb surplus neutrons and pull $k$ back to 1, coolant carries away the heat released because every fission is still happening at the same rate, and withdrawing the rods or removing the moderator lets $k$ run away.
Marking: the 7-8 band needs all three requirements stated for both cases and the linkage explained; 5-6 needs both descriptions without the linkage.

items: 7–8 marks: a well-constructed extensive answer describing the requirements for a controlled nuclear chain reaction AND for an uncontrolled nuclear reaction, showing the linkage between the factors involved in the controlled and uncontrolled reactions.

5–6 marks: a sound answer describing the requirements of a controlled nuclear chain reaction in a fission reactor AND the requirements for an uncontrolled nuclear reaction, with no linkage between the factors involved in the two types of reaction.

3–4 marks: a sound answer which describes the requirements for a controlled nuclear chain reaction AND a sound answer which describes the requirements for an uncontrolled chain reaction (or a limited answer for both).

content.text: Use diagrams to describe the variation between digital and analogue voltage outputs with time.

Digital: the output voltage takes only a small number of discrete values, changing in steps (a square or staircase waveform), so the value is always defined to within one step. Analogue: the output voltage takes any value between the limits and varies continuously with time, as a smooth curve.

Put output voltage on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis and draw both traces on the same axes. For the digital system the voltage can take only a small number of defined levels, so the trace jumps between them and is a square or staircase waveform. For the analogue system the voltage takes every value between its limits and varies smoothly with time, so the trace is a smooth curve, for example sinusoidal. content.text: Describe and compare the physical principles underlying the operation of input and output transducers. Use an analogue ammeter and a solar cell as examples.
Classify each device first: does it take energy in and produce an electrical signal, or take an electrical signal and produce something a person can read?
For the ammeter, identify the two energy conversions in series - electrical to mechanical, then mechanical displacement to a readable value.
For the solar cell, identify the specific semiconductor process that converts photons into a potential difference.

An analogue ammeter is an output transducer: it converts electrical energy (current) into a mechanical rotation of a coil in the magnetic field of a permanent magnet, and the deflection of the pointer against a calibrated scale converts this into a readable value. A solar cell is an input transducer: it converts light energy directly into electrical energy when photons are absorbed in a semiconductor, promoting electrons to the conduction band and leaving holes, so a potential difference is set up between the terminals. The comparison is that both depend on energy conversion between different forms - electrical to mechanical in the ammeter, light to electrical in the solar cell - and both may be described as transducers because each converts energy from one form to another in a controlled way; they differ in the direction of conversion, with the ammeter a measuring (output) device and the solar cell a source (input) device. Both also rely on the response of charged particles (electrons) to forces or excitation.

Method: treat this as a two-column table with the same headings for each device - what energy enters, what physical mechanism converts it, and what energy leaves. Write the mechanism in terms of the particles involved, because that is what distinguishes an ammeter from a solar cell.

Test for each device: name the input energy and ask whether the device then supplies energy to a circuit (input transducer) or drains energy from a circuit to produce a movement a person can read (output transducer). Applying that test is the comparison the top band wants, and it also settles the direction of conversion without needing a separate sentence.

The two descriptions have to be genuinely physical, not functional. 'The ammeter uses a magnet' is not enough; the marks are for the motor effect turning a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field, and then the second conversion from that rotation into a deflection against a calibrated scale. 'The solar cell uses light' is not enough; the marks are for photons promoting electrons across the semiconductor band gap and the resulting electron-hole pairs being separated.

The shared thread that makes the comparison worthwhile is that both devices turn on the behaviour of the same charged particles: the ammeter on a current forced through a conductor in a magnetic field, the solar cell on electrons excited by absorbed photons. Two devices that both convert energy, in opposite directions, in response to the same particle.

Marking: 7-8 needs both principles described and the comparison drawn; 5-6 needs both descriptions without the comparison, or one description plus a comparison; 3-4 needs both devices identified and one described.

1–2 marks: correctly identifies the input transducer (solar cell) and/or the output transducer (analogue ammeter).
